name: Vermont
one: Vermont mails a ballot to every registered voter. Below: how to send it back and the deadlines.
sec:
Vote by mail or absentee

Can’t get to your polling place on Election Day? Here is how to vote by mail in Vermont, from the state’s own election office and its laws. Checked October 21, 2026.

Getting your ballot

Monday, November 2Passed

By 5 p.m., or when the town clerk's office closes, on the day before the election: Monday, November 2, 2026. If your clerk's office has no hours that day, the deadline is closing time on the last day it is open before the election. (Rule: the day before the election.) (the law)

Send it back by

Tuesday, November 3Passed

Returned by mail: it must reach the town clerk's office before the polls close on Election Day, Tuesday, November 3, 2026. Handed in at the clerk's office or put in your town's drop box: before the close of business on Monday, November 2, 2026. Brought to your polling place: before 7:00 p.m. on Tuesday, November 3, 2026. (the law)

That date has passed. You can still vote in person, early or on Election Day, Tuesday, November 3.You can still vote in person on Election Day, Tuesday, November 3. Early voting in person runs through Monday, November 2, 2026. When and where to vote early.

Ask for a ballot online, on Vermont’s own site

At school away from home, in Vermont or in another state? What Vermont says about students is under Show more.

Who can vote by mail

No reason is needed. For the general election, the Secretary of State's office mails a ballot to every active registered voter; you do not have to ask for one. Any voter may also ask their town or city clerk for an early (absentee) ballot, for example to have it sent to another address. (official page)

How to ask for a ballot

  • Online. Ask for a ballot through the Vermont Voter Portal. Open it (official page)
  • By mail. Fill out the early/absentee ballot request form and return it to your town or city clerk's office. A request can also be made in writing by a family member or another person you authorize. Open it (official page)
  • In person. Ask at your town or city clerk's office, or by telephone to the clerk. You, a family member or a health care provider acting for you may ask by phone, in person or in writing. (official page)

How to send it back

  • By mail. Mail it back to your town or city clerk in the postage-paid return envelope that came with it. It counts only if it reaches the clerk's office before the polls close on Election Day, so mail it early. (the law)
  • Drop box. Put it in a secure drop box provided by the town or city where you are registered, before the close of business on Monday, November 2, 2026. (the law)
  • In person. Bring it to your town clerk's office during business hours before it closes on Monday, November 2, or hand it to the election officials at your polling place before 7:00 p.m. on Tuesday, November 3, 2026. One person may not return more than 25 ballots. (the law)

What the envelope needs

Sign the certificate on the outside of the ballot envelope, or the ballot will not count. No witness or notary is needed. A voter who cannot sign may mark an X, with the officers who bring the ballot signing as witnesses. If there is a problem, such as an unsigned envelope, the clerk will tell you within three days of receiving it and you can fix it so your ballot counts. (official page)

Track your ballot

Track your ballot on Vermont’s own site (official page)

Vote early in person instead

Saturday, September 19, 2026 to Monday, November 2, 2026.

Vote early at your town or city clerk's office during its business hours. Early voting for the general election starts 45 days before the election (Saturday, September 19, 2026) or as soon as ballots are available, and runs until the clerk's office closes on the day before the election. Clerks' hours differ, so check with yours. (official page)

Students

At school in Vermont, away from home

Vermont law says a person does not gain or lose a residence just by being a student. So a student at a school in another Vermont town may stay registered in the last town where they lived and ask that town's clerk for an absentee ballot. A student may instead register in the town where they now live if they consider it their main home; you must live in the town where you register, and you can be registered in only one place. If your mailing address is different from where you live, give it to the clerk, who uses it to send absentee ballots. (official page)

At school in another state, with Vermont as home

The Secretary of State says a Vermonter living out of state for a while, for example for college, can keep voting in Vermont in the town where they last lived, as long as they consider it their main home and plan to return. Ask that town or city clerk to send an absentee ballot; it can be sent as early as 45 days before the election. A student from another state at a Vermont college may vote in Vermont if they consider Vermont their main home, or may vote in their home state; for that, the Secretary says to check with the home state's election office. (official page)

Military and overseas

Military and overseas voters can register and ask for a ballot through the Vermont Voter Portal, or by telephone, fax, e-mail or mail; the Federal Post Card Application (FPCA) counts as a request. The blank ballot can be sent by e-mail, fax or mail. The Secretary of State says the voted ballot must come back to the town clerk in the signed certificate envelope: it cannot be returned by fax or e-mail. (official page)

Vermont in the Federal Voting Assistance Program’s guide

Good to know

  • The Secretary of State announced on October 7, 2026 that general election ballots had been mailed to all active registered voters. If yours has not come by mid-October, the Secretary asks you to check with your town or city clerk. The Secretary's office recommended mailing a voted ballot back by October 20, two weeks before Election Day, so it arrives in time. The other ways to return it are listed above.
  • If you go to the polls without the ballot that was mailed to you, or you moved within Vermont, you can still vote: you sign an 'Affidavit of No Ballot Cast' and the clerk gives you a new ballot.
  • Vermont's mail ballots go back to your own town or city clerk, not to the state. Clerks' office hours differ from town to town.
  • If you are sick or have a disability, you may ask by 5 p.m. on the day before the election for a ballot to be brought to your home on Election Day by two justices of the peace.

Polls close at 7 p.m. Each town sets its opening time, between 5 and 10 a.m. (the law)

Anyone in line when the polls close may still vote.
